sections.title: From Understanding Zones to Configuring Them
learningObjectives: Recall the zone concepts introduced in L2-M4
Understand the Programmer's role in defining zone behavior
sections.content: L2-M4 introduced shared paths and reserved routes conceptually, as part of understanding fleet coordination. As a Programmer, you actively configure these zones - deciding where traffic should be prioritized, shared, or restricted, based on the facility's actual operational patterns.

keyTerms.note: MoRo's Human-Machine Interface (HMI) platform — introduced in L1-M3.

sections.title: Identifying Zone Requirements
learningObjectives: Understand how to assess a facility for zone configuration needs
Recognize factors that suggest a dedicated zone is needed
sections.content: Zone configuration starts with understanding the facility's actual traffic patterns - areas with high fleet density, narrow passages where simultaneous multi-unit traffic would be problematic, or routes tied to time-sensitive operations that benefit from priority. Not every facility needs extensive zone configuration; simpler layouts with light fleet traffic may work fine with minimal zoning.

video.title: Do you need a zone in 30 seconds
video.transcript: Do you need a zone? In 30 seconds. Start with the facility’s real traffic patterns. Where is fleet density high? Where would several units in a narrow passage be a problem? Which routes are time-sensitive and need priority? Not every facility needs extensive zoning. Light traffic may need only minimal zones.

sections.title: Configuring Shared Paths
learningObjectives: Understand the general configuration approach for a shared path
Recognize what makes a shared path configuration effective
sections.content: A shared path allows multiple units through with automatic coordination - the configuration work involves defining the path boundaries and confirming the coordination logic handles the facility's actual traffic volume without creating unexpected congestion. Specific configuration steps within ANT will be confirmed against the live system.

keyTerms.note: A path that lets several units through with automatic coordination.

sections.title: Configuring Reserved Routes
learningObjectives: Understand the general configuration approach for a reserved route
Recognize appropriate use cases for route reservation versus shared paths
sections.content: A reserved route prioritizes or dedicates a path for specific traffic - appropriate when a particular route is time-sensitive or when a bottleneck location genuinely needs single-unit-at-a-time access rather than coordinated sharing. Over-using reserved routes where shared paths would suffice can create unnecessary rigidity in fleet operations.

keyTerms.note: A path prioritized or dedicated to specific traffic.

sections.title: Testing Zone Configuration
learningObjectives: Understand how to validate zone configuration before full operational reliance
Know that congestion or deadlock tendencies may only appear once more units are active
sections.content: Zone configuration should be tested with realistic traffic volume before being relied upon for daily operation - a configuration that looks fine with one or two units may reveal congestion or deadlock tendencies (covered conceptually in L2-M4) only once more units are active. Testing under realistic load is what surfaces these issues before they become operational problems.

keyTerms.note: Units each waiting for another to move, so none can proceed.

sections.title: Adjusting Zones Over Time
learningObjectives: Understand that zone configuration often needs adjustment as fleet size or layout changes
Recognize indicators that existing zone configuration needs revisiting
sections.content: Zone configuration that worked well for a smaller fleet may need adjustment as more units are added, or as facility layout changes shift traffic patterns. Signs worth watching for - increasing congestion reports, growing deadlock frequency - indicate it's worth revisiting the zone configuration rather than treating it as a one-time setup.

questions.question: What should zone decisions be based on?
options: The facility's actual operational traffic patterns
The same layout used at the previous site
The order in which units joined the fleet
questions.feedback: Correct. Programmers configure zone behavior based on the facility's actual traffic patterns.

questions.question: Which facility is most likely to work with minimal zoning?
options: Narrow passages and high fleet density
A simpler layout with light fleet traffic
questions.feedback: Correct. Zone configuration needs scale with actual traffic complexity, not a fixed requirement.

questions.question: A path carries steady traffic from several units, is not time-sensitive, and is not a bottleneck. Which choice fits the lesson?
options: A reserved route, to be safe
A shared path, because reserved routes suit time-sensitive routes and bottlenecks
Reserve every route on that side of the facility
questions.feedback: Correct. Reserved routes suit specific time-sensitive or bottleneck scenarios, not general use.

questions.question: A zone configuration ran without problems in a test with two units. What can you conclude?
options: It is ready for daily operation
It is not yet proven; congestion or deadlock tendencies may appear only with more units active
questions.feedback: Correct. Issues that don't appear with one or two units may surface under realistic fleet volume.

questions.question: Which is a sign that zone configuration needs revisiting?
questions.feedback: Correct. Growing congestion or deadlock frequency signals a need to revisit zone configuration.
